source_text: Edam jam nunc ego ipsa negotia christianae factionis, ut qui mala refutaverim, bona ostendam. Corpus sumus de conscientia religionis et disciplinae divinitate et spei foedere. Coimus in coetum et congregationem, ut ad Deum, quasi manu facta, precationibus ambiamus. Haec vis Deo grata est. Oramus etiam pro imperatoribus, pro ministeriis eorum ac potestatibus, pro statu seculi, pro rerum quiete, pro mora finis. Cogimur ad litterarum divinarum commemorationem, si quid praesentium temporum qualitas aut praemonere cogit aut recognoscere. Certe fidem sanctis vocibus pascimus, spem erigimus, fiduciam figimus, disciplinam praeceptorum nihilominus in compulsationibus densamus; ibidem etiam exhortationnes, castigationnes et censura divina. Nam et judicatur magno cum pondere, ut apud certos de Dei conspectu, summumque futuri judicii praejudicium est, si quis ita deliquerit, ut a communicatione orationis et conventus et omnis sancti commercii relegetur, Praesident probati quique seniores, honorem istum non pretio sed testimonio adepti; neque enim pretio ulla res Dei constat. Etiam si quod arcae genus est, non de honoraria summa, quasi redemptae religionis congregatur; modicam unusquisque stipem menstrua die, vel quum velit, et si modo velit et si modo possit, apponit: nam nemo compellitur, sed sponte confert. Haec quasi deposita pietatis sunt. Nam inde non epulis nec potaculis, nec ingratis voratrinis dispensatur, sed egenis alendis humandisque, et pueris ac puellis re ac parentibus destitutis, jamque domesticis senibus, item naufragis, et si qui in metallis, et si qui in insulis, vel in custodiis, duntaxat ex caussa Dei sectae alumni confessionis suae fiunt. Sed ejusmodi vel maxime dilectionis operatio notam nobis inurit penes quosdam. Vide, inquiunt, ut invicem se diligant: ipsi enim invicem oderunt; et ut pro alterutro mori sint parati: ipsi enim ad occidendum alterutrum paratiores erunt. Sed et quod fratrum appellatione censemur, non alias, opinor, infamant, quam quod apud ipsos omne sanguinis nomen de affectatione simulatum est. Fratres autem etiam vestri sumus, jure naturae matris unius, etsi vos parum homines, quia mali fratres. At quanto dignius fratres et dicuntur et habentur, qui unum patrem Deum agnoverunt, qui unum Spiritum biberunt sanctitatis, qui de uno utero ignorantiae ejusdem ad unam lucem expaverunt veritatis. Sed eo fortasse minus legitimi existimamur, quia nulla de nostra fraternitate tragoedia exclamat, vel quia ex substantia familiari fratres sumus, quae penes vos fere dirimit fraternitatem. Itaque qui animo animaque miscemur, nihil de rei communicatione dubitamus. Omnia indiscreta sunt apud nos, praeter uxores: in isto loco consortium solvimus, in quo solo caeteri homines consortium exercent, qui non amicorum solummodo matrimonia usurpant, sed et sua amicis patientissime subministrant, ex illa, credo, majorum et sapientissimorum disciplina, Graeci Socratis et Romani Catonis, qui uxores suas amicis communicaverunt, quas in matrimonium duxerant liberorum caussa et alibi creandorum, nescio quidem an invitas; quid enim de castitate curarent, quam mariti tam facile donaverant? O sapientiae Atticae, o Romanae gravitatis exemplum! Leno est philosophus et censor. Quid ergo mirum, si tanta caritas convivatur? Nam et coenulas nostras, praeterquam sceleris infames, ut prodigas quoque suggillatis. De nobis scilicet Diogenis dictum est: Megarenses obsonant quasi crastina die morituri, aedificant vero quasi nunquam morituri. Sed stipulam quis in alieno oculo facilius perspicit, quam in suo trabem. Tot tribubus et curiis et decuriis ructantibus acescit aër. Saliis coenaturis creditor erit necessarius. Herculanarum decimarum et polluctorum sumptus tabularii supputabant. Apaturiis, Dionysiis, mysteriis Atticis coquorum delectus indicentur. Ad fumum coenae Serapiacae sparteoli excitabuntur. De solo triclinio Christianorum retractatur, Coena nostra de nomine rationem sui ostendit; id vocatur, quod dilectio penes Graecos est. Quantiscumque sumptibus constet, lucrum est pietatis nomine facere sumptum, siquidem inopes quosque refrigerio isto juvamus, non qua penes vos parasiti affectant ad gloriam famulandae libertatis sub auctoramento ventris inter contumelias saginandi, sed qua penes Deum major est contemplatio mediocrium. Si honesta caussa est convivii, reliquum ordinem disciplinae aestimate, qui sit de religionnis officio: nihil vilitatis, nihil immodestiae admittit; non prius discumbitur, quam oratio ad Deum praegustetur; editur quantum esurientes capiunt; bibitur quantum pudicis est utile. Ita saturantur, ut qui meminerint etiam per noctem adorandum Deum sibi esse; ita fabulantur, ut qui sciant dominum audire. Post aquam manualem et lumina, ut quisque de scripturis sanctis vel de proprio ingenio potest provocatur in medium Deo canere hinc probatur quomodo biberit. Oeque oratio convivium dirimit. Inde disceditur non in catervas caesionum neque n classes discursationum, nec in eruptiones lasciviarum, sed ad eamdem curam modestiae et pudicitiae ut qui non tam coenam coenaverint, quam disciplinam. Haec coitio christianorum merito sane illicita, si illicitis pari merito damnanda, [si non dissimilis damnandis,] si quis de ea queritur eo titulo, quo de factionibus querela est. In cujus perniciem aliquando convenimus? Hoc sumus congregati, quod et dispersi; hoc universi, quod et singuli; neminem laedentes, neminem contristantes. Quum probi, quum boni coeunt, quum pii, quum casti congregantur, non est factio dicenda, sed curia.
pass_a_gloss: Now I will already set forth the affairs of the Christian faction, so that, having refuted the evils, I may show the goods. We are a body from the conscience of religion and the divinity of discipline and the covenant of hope. We come together into a gathering and congregation, so that, as if with one hand, we may go around to God with prayers. This power is pleasing to God. We also pray for the emperors, for their ministries and powers, for the state of the world, for the quiet of things, for the delay of the end. We are compelled to the remembrance of divine letters, if the quality of present times thinks to warn or recognize something. Certainly, we nourish faith with holy voices, we raise up hope, we fix confidence, we thicken discipline with the compulsions of precepts; also there are exhortations, castigations, and divine censures there. For it is judged with great weight, so that, as if before certain ones from God's sight, it is the greatest prejudice of future judgment, if someone has delinqued in such a way that he is released from the communication of prayer and gathering and all holy commerce. The proven elders preside, having obtained this honor not with a price, but with testimony; for no affair of God is constituted with a price. Also, if there is some kind of money box, it is not gathered from an honorary sum, as if for a redeemed religion; each one puts a small monthly stipend on a certain day, or when he wishes, and if only he wishes and if only he is able: for no one is compelled, but he contributes spontaneously. These are like deposits of piety. For from there, it is not dispensed for feasts nor drinks nor ungrateful voraciousness, but for nourishing and burying the needy, and for boys and girls who are destitute of resources and parents, and now for domestic elders, also for shipwrecked ones, and if there are any in mines, and if there are any on islands, or in custodies, provided that they become pupils of the confession of God's sect for this cause. But such an operation of love brands a note for us among certain ones. See, they say, how they love one another: for they themselves hate one another; and how they are prepared to die for one another: for they themselves are more prepared to kill one another. But also because we are counted with the appellation of brothers, I think they do not defame us, except that among them every name of blood is simulated from affection. But we are also your brothers, by the right of nature of one mother, although you are hardly men, because you are evil brothers. But how much more worthy are those who are called and considered brothers, who have recognized one God the Father, who have drunk one Holy Spirit of sanctity, who have been frightened from one womb of ignorance to one light of truth. But perhaps we are considered less legitimate, because no tragedy of our brotherhood cries out, or because we are brothers from a familial substance, which almost destroys brotherhood among you. And so, those who are mixed with soul and spirit, we do not doubt anything about the communication of things. All things are indiscriminate among us, except for wives: in this place, we dissolve the partnership, in which alone other men exercise partnership, who not only usurp the marriages of friends, but also patiently provide their own wives to friends, from that, I believe, discipline of the greater and wisest ones, the Greek Socrates and the Roman Cato, who communicated their wives to friends, whom they had led into marriage for the sake of children and to be created elsewhere; I do not know, indeed, whether unwillingly; for what did they care about chastity, which husbands had easily given away? O example of Attic wisdom, O example of Roman gravity! The philosopher is a pimp and a censor. What, therefore, is surprising, if such great love is feasted? For also our dinners, except for those infamous of crime, even those prodigal ones are reproached. Certainly, the saying of Diogenes was said about us: The Megarians dine as if they will die tomorrow, but they build as if they will never die. But who can more easily see a straw in someone else's eye than a beam in his own? The air grows thick with so many tribes and curias and decurias belching. A necessary creditor will be for the salty dinners. The sum of the expenses of the Herculan tables and the pollutions are calculated by the accountants. The choice of cooks is indicated for the Apaturian, Dionysian, and Attic mysteries. The sparteoli are excited for the smoke of the Serapian dinner. But only the triclinium of the Christians is criticized; our dinner shows its reason from its name; it is called what love is among the Greeks. However much it may cost with expenses, it is a gain to make an expense in the name of piety, since we help all the needy with this refreshment, not as the parasites among you affect for the glory of serving liberty under the authorization of the belly, being fed among insults, but as it is greater among God to consider the mediocre. If the cause of the dinner is honest, estimate the remaining order of discipline, which is from the office of religion: it does not admit anything vile, anything immodest; one does not recline before prayer is tasted to God; one eats as much as the hungry take; one drinks as much as is useful to the chaste. Thus they are satisfied, so that they may remember even through the night to adore God for themselves; thus they talk, so that they may know the Lord is hearing. After the hand-washing and the lights, as each one is able from the holy scriptures or from his own talent, he is provoked to sing to God in the midst; thus it is proven how he has drunk. And then prayer dissolves the dinner. From there, they depart not into crowds of caesions nor into classes of discourses, nor into eruptions of lasciviousness, but to the same care of modesty and chastity, as if they have not dined so much as they have disciplined. This gathering of Christians is rightly illicit, if it is to be condemned with equal merit, if someone complains about it with that title, with which a complaint is about factions. Against whose ruin do we ever gather? We are gathered for this, which we are also when dispersed; this is universal, which is also singular; we harm no one, we grieve no one. When the good, when the upright, when the pious, when the chaste gather, it is not to be called a faction, but a curia.
pass_b_english: I will now lay out the business of the Christian faction so that, having refuted the charges, I can show the virtues. We are a body formed by religious conscience, divine discipline, and the covenant of hope. We assemble as a congregation to approach God with prayers, as if with one hand, and this power pleases God. We also pray for emperors, their officials and authority, for the state of the world, for peace, and for the delay of the end. We are driven to rehearse the divine letters whenever the character of the present age demands warning or recognition. We nourish faith with holy words, lift hope, anchor confidence, and tighten discipline through the compulsions of precept; here too we find exhortations, castigations, and divine censure. Judgment is carried out with great weight, as if before certain ones in God's sight, and it serves as the highest prejudgment of the future judgment: if anyone so offends that he is cut off from the communion of prayer, assembly, and all holy fellowship. Proven elders preside, having earned this honor not by purchase but by testimony, for no affair of God is established by a price. Even if there is a money box, it is not funded by honorary fees as if religion were for sale; each person contributes a small monthly amount on a set day, or whenever he wishes, and only if he wishes and is able, for no one is compelled, but all give freely. These are like deposits of piety. From them, nothing is spent on feasts, drinking bouts, or wasteful gluttony, but on feeding and burying the needy, on boys and girls deprived of means and parents, on elderly household members, on shipwreck victims, on those in mines, on islands, or in prisons, provided they suffer for the sake of confessing God's sect. Yet this very practice of love brands us in the eyes of some. "See," they say, "how they love one another"—when they themselves hate one another; "and how they are ready to die for one another"—when they are more ready to kill one another. They also slander us for bearing the name of brothers, I think, only because among them every claim of blood kinship is simulated from pretense. We are your brothers too, by nature's right from one mother, though you are barely human because you are evil brothers. But how much worthier are those called and treated as brothers who have acknowledged one Father God, who have drunk one Spirit of holiness, who have been startled from one womb of ignorance into one light of truth. Perhaps we seem less legitimate because no tragedy of our brotherhood cries out, or because we are brothers by family substance, which among you nearly destroys brotherhood. Therefore we who are mingled in soul and spirit have no doubt about sharing our goods. All things are common among us, except wives. We dissolve the partnership in the very place where other men exercise it—men who not only usurp their friends' marriages but also obligingly provide their own wives to friends, following, I believe, the discipline of the greatest and wisest, the Greek Socrates and the Roman Cato, who shared their wives with friends—wives they had married for children and for begetting them elsewhere; I do not know whether unwillingly, for what did they care about chastity when husbands gave it away so easily? O example of Attic wisdom, O example of Roman gravity! The philosopher acts as pimp and censor. So why wonder if such great love is feasted? Even our dinners, infamous only to criminals, you brand as prodigal. The saying of Diogenes was spoken of us: "The Megarians dine as if they will die tomorrow, but build as if they will never die." But who sees a straw in another's eye more easily than a beam in his own? The air grows thick with so many tribes, curiae, and decuriae belching. A necessary creditor awaits the Salian feasts. Accountants tally the expenses of Herculean tables and pollutions. Cooks are selected for the Apaturian, Dionysian, and Attic mysteries. Sparteoli are kindled for the smoke of the Serapian dinner. Yet only the Christian triclinium is criticized. Our dinner shows its reason in its name: it is called by the Greek word for love. Whatever the cost, it is gain to spend in the name of piety, since we refresh all the needy—not as parasites among you who perform service for the glory of liberty under the authorization of the belly, fattening themselves on insults—but because the contemplation of the humble is greater before God. If the cause of the dinner is honest, judge the rest of its discipline as a religious duty: it admits nothing base, nothing immodest; no one reclines before prayer has been tasted to God; each eats as much as hunger takes, drinks as much as chastity finds useful. They are satisfied so as to remember even through the night that they must adore God; they speak as those who know the Lord is listening. After hand-washing and lamps, each is prompted to sing to God from the holy scriptures or his own talent, and thus it is proven how he has drunk. Then prayer dismisses the dinner. They depart not into crowds of the blue-clad, nor into classes of discourse, nor into eruptions of lust, but to the same care for modesty and chastity, as if they have not so much dined as disciplined. This Christian gathering is rightly called illicit only if it deserves condemnation on the same grounds as illicit gatherings—if anyone complains of it under the same title used against factions. Against whose ruin do we ever convene? We gather for this very reason: we are gathered even when dispersed; this unity is universal because it is also singular; we harm no one, we grieve no one. When the upright, the good, the pious, the chaste assemble, it is not to be called a faction, but a senate.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex rhetorical structure and the specific cultural references (Socrates, Cato, Diogenes). Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Locked Latin. All clauses, including the conditional and comparative structures, are preserved. Scripture references are not present in the source text, so none were required/added.
